### Advanced research budget (MONEY-1159)

| Source File                                | Test File                                                           | Test Cases | Status |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ------ |
| `workers/src/processors/research-logic.ts` | `apps/web/__tests__/workers/research.test.ts`                       | +3         | PASS   |
| (same)                                     | `workers/__tests__/processors/processor-boundary-contracts.test.ts` | +1         | PASS   |

`resolveResearchMode` recognised only `"deep"`, and nothing in the repo has ever
published that: `ResearchJobMessage.mode` is `"fast" | "advanced"`, and the UI
style called "deep" is mapped to `"advanced"` before publish
(`mapStyleToMode`). Every advanced run therefore fell through to `"fast"` →
FAST_AGENT_CONFIG (120s) → a **180s** processor hard ceiling. The agent DID
reconfigure itself to 480s at `run()` time, but the processor's `Promise.race`
killed it at 180s regardless — so advanced research got roughly a quarter of its
budget and failed looking like an ordinary timeout rather than a
misconfiguration.

Fixing the mode fixes the ceiling with no separate change: `"advanced"` now
selects ADVANCED_AGENT_CONFIG (480s), and `computeResearchHardCeiling(480s)` is
`min(480+60, 540) = 540s`, which no longer undercuts the agent.

The two `ResearchMode` unions (worker `"fast" | "deep"`, canonical
`"fast" | "advanced"`) are deliberately KEPT, with `toAgentResearchMode` as the
tested bridge. The divergence was never the bug — refusing the value publishers
actually send was. `"deep"` stays accepted as a legacy alias so a message
already in the subscription at deploy time resolves to the mode it was
published for.

Two tests had to CHANGE rather than be added, and both were written in
anticipation of exactly this:

- `processor-boundary-contracts.test.ts` carried a case named "every real
  payload mode still resolves to fast — **the known open bug**", pinning the
  defect on purpose so it stayed visible. Its own comment said it should go red
  and be updated when the runtime fix landed. It did, and it was — not
  weakened, re-pointed at the correct behaviour.
- `research.test.ts` had no case for `"advanced"` at all. The ABSENT assertion
  was the bug; adding it is the regression.

The chain case is the one that matters: it walks published mode → worker label →
agent mode → config → ceiling and asserts 540s, explicitly rejecting 180s. A
mapping assertion alone would not have caught the damage, since the mapping is
only interesting because of the budget it selects. A companion case pins that
fast jobs still get 120s/180s, so the fix cannot degenerate into a blanket
raise that hides genuinely stuck fast runs.

### Sign-out drops the persisted plan (MONEY-1134)

| Source File                               | Test File                                                      | Test Cases | Status |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ------ |
| `apps/web/lib/auth/sign-out.ts`           | `apps/web/__tests__/subscription/sign-out-clears-plan.test.ts` | 4          | PASS   |
| `apps/web/lib/subscription/plan-cache.ts` | (same)                                                         | —          | PASS   |

`clearCachedPlan()` is documented as "the sign-out path" and was built for it —
it clears the in-memory value, drops `um_plan_v1` from localStorage, and bumps a
generation so a fetch already in flight cannot write the old plan back. It had
**zero production call sites**. Tests only. So the persisted plan outlived the
session and, on a shared browser, the next person hydrated the previous user's
billing tier.

Not a privilege escalation — `entitlement-isolation.test.ts` pins that no gate
reads this value; it feeds the sidebar tier chip and some walkthrough copy. It
is still someone else's billing tier rendered as yours on a machine they no
longer have a session on.

Now cleared on all four sign-out paths: `instantSignOut` (Sidebar +
PlayfulHeader), `SessionGuard`'s ghosted-session force-signout,
`TermsAcceptanceModal`'s decline, and both exits in `DeleteAccountDialog`.

The guard walks EVERY `signOut(` call site under `app/`, `components/` and
`lib/` and requires each to clear the plan or delegate to `instantSignOut`. That
is the shape the defect demanded: it was an ABSENT call, and it survived because
nothing connected "a function documented for sign-out" to "the code that signs
out". The guard proved its worth on first run by finding a call site the manual
sweep had missed — `DeleteAccountDialog`, which is the strongest case in the
ticket, since the user has just asked for everything about them to be deleted.

Two cases guard the guard: a sanity check that call sites are found at all (a
walker that sees nothing would pass vacuously — the same shape as the original
bug), and one pinning that `clearCachedPlan` still does all three of its jobs,
without which every call site above becomes decorative. A fourth pins that the
clear runs BEFORE the session is revoked rather than inside the promise chain
that races a hard navigation.

The main body of MONEY-1134 — invalidating the server-side entitlement cache on
every subscription mutation — was already done via the shared
`invalidateEntitlement` helper (13 sites across `subscription.service.ts`,
`subscription-grants.service.ts`, `scheduled-plan-changes.service.ts`). This was
the ticket's remaining secondary item.

### Sector tombstone guard widened to the whole tree (MONEY-1152)

| Source File                                 | Test File                                                    | Test Cases | Status |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------- | ------ |
| all `apps/`, `packages/`, `workers/` source | `packages/services/__tests__/holdings-sector-shadow.test.ts` | +3         | PASS   |

`sector: { not: null }` counts the `"N/A"` tombstone (`SECTOR_SKIPPED`) as a
real sector. Measured on the QA DB: 21,885 of 22,153 active EQUITY instruments
are non-null, but **14,893 of those are the sentinel** — genuinely classified is
6,992 (31.6%), not 98.8%. In a sector aggregate that bucket does not merely add
noise, it can dominate and dwarf every real sector.

The six known sites were already fixed to use `REAL_SECTOR_WHERE`, and a guard
already existed — but it scanned a hard-coded list of five files. That cannot
catch the seventh, which matters because six is how many there already were: the
naive form reads as obviously correct, so it kept being written independently
across two apps by people with no reason to consult a list inside a test file.
An allow-list guard only protects files someone already thought to add.

Now walks `apps/`, `packages/` and `workers/` instead. Mutation-verified by
injecting the naive filter into `peers-sync.service.ts` — a file the old
allow-list did not cover — which the widened scan flags and the old one would
have missed entirely.

`dist` and `build` are skipped deliberately: compiled output carries the old
text and would report violations nobody can fix in source. Comments are
stripped first (LINE before BLOCK, MONEY-1143) so the several files that
DOCUMENT this hazard are not mistaken for committing it, and the test excludes
itself since it holds the pattern as a regex and as fixtures.

Two meta cases guard the guard: a liveness floor (500+ files, or the walker is
blind) and a pattern check confirming it flags the naive form, ignores
`REAL_SECTOR_WHERE`, and does not fire on a `not: null` filter over a DIFFERENT
field.

Left open and tracked separately as MONEY-1172: **why** 67% of the universe is
unresolvable. A tombstone is terminal — enrichment only fetches rows with NO
sector, so `"N/A"` rows are permanently excluded from future attempts and
coverage cannot recover on its own.

### Webhook/callback grant parity (MONEY-1063)

| Source File                                            | Test File                                                    | Test Cases | Status |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------- | ------ |
| `packages/services/src/subscription-grants.service.ts` | `apps/web/__tests__/api/subscription-grants-service.test.ts` | 19 (0 new) | PASS   |

The webhook grant read `aiQueriesLimit` from the legacy `WEBHOOK_PLANS`
(PRO→10) while the callback grant, provisioning the SAME payment, read
`PLAN_CONFIG` (PRO→20). Whichever path won the `appliedAt` claim decided how
many AI queries a paying PRO user received — an entitlement settled by a race.
Nothing surfaced it: both writes succeed and 10 is a plausible number.

`PLAN_CONFIG` is canonical, and every OTHER limit on that same write object
already read from it (`fastQueries`, `advancedQueries`, `credits` all use
`planConfig`). `aiQueriesLimit` was the lone holdout.

**No new test cases — an existing assertion moved.** The suite pinned
`aiQueriesLimit === 10` deliberately, to keep a known divergence visible rather
than implied, and its header said so. That is the correct use of a pinning test,
and the correct response to fixing the underlying defect is to move the
assertion with it, not to delete it. Same pattern as the MONEY-1159 boundary
contract earlier in this file.

`billingPeriod` divergence #2 is deliberately NOT fixed and is now documented at
the write site. The webhook writes `isRecurring ? period : null`, the callback
writes `(PREMIUM|ULTIMATE|PRO) ? period : null`. `isRecurring` is derived from
`ctx.period`, not the webhook payload, so both paths do have the same
information — but the rules ask different questions ("is the period a real
billing period" vs "is this a subscription plan") and differ for a QUERY_PACK
carrying a period and for a subscription plan carrying an odd one. The correct
rule is arguably the conjunction, which is a third behaviour: a semantic
decision on a live billing field rather than a unification, and unlike
`aiQueriesLimit` there is no canonical source to point at.

### /v1 coverage measured per ENDPOINT + the turn contract (MONEY-1091)

| Source File                                            | Test File                                                        | Test Cases | Status |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ------ |
| `apps/api/src/routes/v1/*.ts`                          | `apps/api/__tests__/meta/endpoint-contract-coverage.test.ts`     | 7          | PASS   |
| `apps/api/src/routes/v1/fire.ts`                       | `apps/api/__tests__/routes/fire-turn-contract.test.ts`           | 9          | PASS   |
| `apps/api/src/routes/v1/fire.ts`                       | `apps/api/__tests__/routes/fire-crud-contract.test.ts`           | 12         | PASS   |
| `apps/api/src/routes/v1/notifications.ts`              | `apps/api/__tests__/routes/notifications-contract.test.ts`       | 13         | PASS   |
| `apps/api/src/routes/v1/{paper,research,watchlist}.ts` | `apps/api/__tests__/routes/delete-endpoints-contract.test.ts`    | 21         | PASS   |
| `apps/api/src/routes/v1/{trades,subscription}.ts`      | `apps/api/__tests__/routes/trades-subscription-contract.test.ts` | 11         | PASS   |
| `apps/api/src/routes/v1/market.ts` (`/us/quotes`)      | `apps/api/__tests__/routes/market-us-quotes-contract.test.ts`    | 20         | PASS   |
| `apps/api/src/routes/v1/*.ts`                          | `apps/api/__tests__/meta/service-failure-status-mapping.test.ts` | 5          | PASS   |

The contract suite references all 38 mounted `/v1` families, and that was cited
as evidence the API was covered. Per ENDPOINT the picture differed:
**214 endpoints, 31 untested — 86% covered.** Part 1 closed the most important
one; the FIRE CRUD trio closed three more, the four `/v1/notifications`
endpoints another four, and every remaining DELETE another four; `POST /v1/trades`
and the two subscription reads closed three more — leaving **16 untested —
93%**. What is left is reads only: no DELETEs, no POSTs, no PUTs.

The remaining list is worked in RISK order, not alphabetically: writes and
deletes before reads. A regression in a read shows up on the next screen load;
a regression in a delete does not show up at all. Five of the 27 are DELETEs.

`POST /v1/fire/:id/turn` was the endpoint the ticket was filed for: the newest
one, and the only `/v1` route that mutates a saved plan, calls a model AND
charges credits — guarding a permanent-data-loss path (a chat turn loading a
different saved scenario could overwrite the scenario named in the URL). It
shipped with a disclosed "no automated regression test" gap, and nothing forced
the issue because the FAMILY was already referenced.

Four enumerator defects had to be fixed before the allow-list could be trusted —
each produced phantom gaps or false comfort, and each is pinned by its own meta
case:

1. Route paths must start with `/`. Hono's `c.get("userId")` matches the same
   shape as a registration and invented endpoints like `GET /v1/meuserId`.
2. Mount paths come from `index.ts`, not filenames — `watchlist.ts` mounts at
   `/watchlists`, `quiz.ts` at `/quizzes`.
3. `index.ts` is not a family; its routes live at `/v1`.
4. 21 call sites drive routes with template literals, invisible to a
   double-quote-only scan.

Matching is method-aware, and `GET /v1/research` is why: the suite drives that
exact path seven times, all POST. A path-only matcher would call it covered.

Validated in BOTH directions before the 30 known gaps were listed — every
flagged endpoint confirmed to have zero matching `app.request` calls, several
unflagged ones confirmed to have some. Two further cases guard the list itself:
an entry that becomes covered must be removed, and an entry matching no
registered route is dead weight (that one would have caught the `/v1/watchlist`
phantoms).

`POST /v1/fire/:id/turn` is deliberately NOT in KNOWN_GAPS — it is asserted by
name, the pattern `premium-actions-gated.test.ts` uses for MONEY-1149, so the
endpoint the ticket exists for stays legible instead of being absorbed into a
list of 30. That case is now INVERTED: it asserts coverage, and deleting it once
green would hand back the exact blind spot the ticket removed. The
TICKET_ENDPOINT exemption was also dropped from the main guard, so losing this
coverage trips both cases, not one.

Mutation-verified per the ticket's acceptance criterion: adding a dummy
`GET /v1/fire/dummy-uncovered` fails the suite naming that exact route; removing
`fire-turn-contract.test.ts` fails both the main guard and the named assertion.

#### Part 1 — the `/turn` route contract (9 cases)

Only the LLM boundary (`makeApiFireGenerate`) is stubbed. The real parser, tool
executor, `ServerFireActions` plan and `createScenarioOps` retargeting all run,
so "which tier handled this request" is a genuine outcome rather than something
the test dictates — which matters because that one branch decides both the
reported `source` and whether the caller is BILLED.

| Invariant     | What is asserted                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| tiering       | "retire at 45" takes the free path — asserted as ZERO model hops, not as `source == "deterministic"`                                                                                               |
| credit        | a pure-answer LLM turn charges `fire_chat` once; a tool-calling LLM turn is FREE (billing it would charge users for edits)                                                                         |
| retargeting   | "load Conservative" against `/v1/fire/sc_path/turn` persists to `sc_other`, asserting the target id AND the loaded values — the id alone passes even if the wrong plan is written to the right row |
| failure modes | 401 unauth, 400 malformed/empty/oversize (before any query or model hop), 404 absent vs 500 DB error, 402 on exhausted credits (with the generated text withheld), 500 on a failed persist         |

Mutation-verified against the real route: reverting the retarget to the path
scenario, charging every LLM turn, and turning the 404 into a 500 each produce
exactly one failure.

#### FIRE CRUD — `GET /v1/fire`, `POST /v1/fire`, `PUT /v1/fire/:id` (12 cases)

Create and update are THE SAME service call, discriminated only by arity:

```
POST /v1/fire      → saveFireScenario(userId, body)              // create
PUT  /v1/fire/:id  → saveFireScenario(userId, body, scenarioId)  // update
```

Nothing in the type system separates them — the third parameter is optional —
so "did an id reach the service" is the whole difference between inserting a
scenario and overwriting one. Asserted both ways: POST must call with NO third
argument even when the BODY carries an `id` (otherwise
`POST /v1/fire {id: <someone's row>}` overwrites it), and PUT must pass the
PATH id, never the body's.

The status mapping is the other half, and it differs per route because create
has no not-found path:

| code        | POST          | PUT |
| ----------- | ------------- | --- |
| `NOT_FOUND` | (unreachable) | 404 |
| `INTERNAL`  | 500           | 500 |
| anything    | 400           | 400 |

`GET /v1/fire/:id` carries a comment that its 404 and 500 were once INVERTED (a
DB error 404'd, a missing scenario 200'd with `data: null`). That endpoint is
covered elsewhere; the same inversion is now pinned on the list and update
paths, where nothing was watching. `GET /v1/fire` also asserts that an empty
list is a 200 `[]` — a 404 there makes a new user's empty state
indistinguishable from a broken account.

Mutation-verified: leaking the body's `id` into the update-target slot fails 2
cases, mapping PUT's `NOT_FOUND` to 500 fails 1, and answering 200 instead of
201 on create fails 2.

#### Notifications — and the bug the coverage found (13 cases)

Covers `GET /v1/notifications`, `PATCH /v1/notifications/:id/read`,
`POST /v1/notifications/read-all` and `DELETE /v1/notifications/read`.

`PATCH /:id/read` was **broken** (MONEY-1178, fixed here). It mapped every
service failure to 404, which is inverted and provably so from the service:
`markAsRead` is `updateMany({ where: { id, userId } })`, and Prisma's
`updateMany` does not throw when it matches nothing — it returns `{ count: 0 }`.
So a missing or FOREIGN id took the SUCCESS path, and `success: false` was only
ever reachable from a real DB exception. The 404 therefore never meant "no such
notification"; it meant "the database just failed", dressed as the one status
that tells a client to stop retrying. The notification stayed unread and no
retry fixed it. Now a 500.

A no-op still answers 200, deliberately — mark-as-read is idempotent and the
service does not surface the matched count. MONEY-1179 records that decision.

The list endpoint is offset-backed behind an opaque cursor, so the cursor is
asserted to ROUND-TRIP: the value handed out is fed into a second request and
the skip the service receives is checked (`skip=5`). Without that, a client
silently re-reads page 1 forever. A garbage cursor falls back to page 1 rather
than 500ing, and a short page hands out no cursor at all.

Mutation-verified: restoring the 404 fails exactly one case.

#### Every remaining DELETE, and the second 404/500 bug (21 cases)

Covers `DELETE /v1/paper/:id`, `DELETE /v1/research/:sessionId`,
`DELETE /v1/watchlists/:id` and `DELETE /v1/watchlists/:id/items/:itemId` in ONE
file rather than four. What matters about a delete is not which resource it
removes — it is that every one is **scoped to the authenticated caller** and
that **a failure is reported honestly**. Those invariants are identical across
all four, so a new DELETE that forgets either is visibly inconsistent with its
siblings instead of merely untested.

All four had MONEY-1180: the route mapped every `success: false` to 404, while
every service collapsed TWO outcomes into it — the ownership gate failing
(genuinely not found) and the `catch` around the Prisma call (the DB failed). A
transient DB error therefore answered 404, which tells the client the row is
gone and retrying is pointless. The row is still there; the user presses delete
again and gets the same 404. The services now tag `NOT_FOUND` / `INTERNAL`
(`code` was already optional on `ServiceResult`, so this is additive), and the
routes map `INTERNAL` to 500 with 404 kept as the default for any un-coded path.

Ownership is asserted too: each route must pass the AUTHENTICATED caller, never
anything client-supplied. MONEY-594 and MONEY-620 were real IDOR bugs here, and
a route that forwarded a body/query userId would re-open them with every
service test still green.

A note recorded by the tests: `DELETE /v1/watchlists/:id/items/:itemId` passes
only the ITEM id to the service — the watchlist id in the path does not scope
the removal. Safe today because the item lookup is itself owner-scoped, pinned
so the asymmetry is deliberate.

Mutation-verified: reverting ONE route to the old shape fails 2 cases — its own,
plus the family-shape assertion that catches the odd one out.

#### The last write, the money reads, and a THIRD 404/400 bug (11 cases)

Covers `POST /v1/trades`, `GET /v1/subscription` and
`GET /v1/subscription/payments`.

`POST /v1/trades` had MONEY-1181: every service failure became **400
VALIDATION_ERROR**, which it can never be. The body is validated against
`TradeFormSchema` three lines earlier, and `createTrade` has exactly ONE failure
return — the `catch` around the Prisma write. So `success: false` is always a
server error, and the route answered "Invalid trade". 4xx means "your request
was bad, fix it"; the client does not retry, it shows a validation message, and
the user is asked to correct data that was already correct while the trade is
lost. Now a 500. The genuine 400s — a body failing the schema, and malformed
JSON — are asserted separately so the fix cannot be misread as "trades never
400".

That is the THIRD instance of one pattern on this branch: a route collapses
"the request was bad" and "we failed" into a single branch and picks the client
status.

| Ticket     | Endpoint(s)                        | Reported as |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------- |
| MONEY-1178 | `PATCH /v1/notifications/:id/read` | 404         |
| MONEY-1180 | all four `/v1` DELETEs             | 404         |
| MONEY-1181 | `POST /v1/trades`                  | 400         |

The subscription reads are pinned to FAIL LOUD, which is the opposite of their
sibling `GET /v1/subscription/access`. That endpoint deliberately fails-to-FREE
with a 200 so a DB blip cannot lock a user out — correct for an entitlement
GATE, wrong for these two. Telling a paying user they are on FREE because a
query failed is a billing-grade lie, and a payment history that renders as "no
payments" during an outage is indistinguishable from having none. Both are
asserted to 500, and the empty-list case is asserted to stay a real 200 `[]` so
the two can never collapse into each other.

Mutation-verified: restoring the 400 fails one case; making
`GET /v1/subscription` fail-to-FREE fails one.

#### The guard for the pattern itself (MONEY-1182, 5 cases)

Three instances of one bug in one branch is a pattern, not a coincidence, so it
is encoded rather than left to be found a fourth time.

**The rule:** if a `/v1` handler branches on `!x.success` and returns any 4xx
from that branch, it must INSPECT `x.code` in the same branch. It deliberately
does not demand a particular status — some services genuinely have only a
not-found failure path and a flat 404 is right there. What it demands is that
the author LOOKED, so the status is a decision rather than a copy of the route
next door.

Branches are keyed `file METHOD /path`, not by line number, so ordinary edits do
not churn the list. Keys AGGREGATE: a route counts as blind while any of its
branches is. `me.ts DELETE /` has two and only one consults `code` — without
aggregation, fixing one would retire the entry and hide the other.

`KNOWN_BLIND` records the 20 pre-existing handlers (MONEY-1183 audits them). It
shrinks and never grows, and is guarded both ways: an entry that starts
inspecting `code` must be removed, and an entry matching no branch is dead
weight. Two meta-cases guard the scanner itself — it must find branches of both
kinds, and the four DELETEs fixed in MONEY-1180 must read as compliant, which is
the positive ground truth that catches a scanner reading the wrong text.

Mutation-verified: reverting one fixed DELETE to the old shape fails 2 cases.

> The table drives each endpoint through a closure whose URL **and** `method`
> literals sit inside the `app.request(...)` call. That is required, not
> stylistic: the coverage guard reads the path from the literal at the call site
> and the method from the text right after it, so `app.request(d.url, init)`
> would drive all four endpoints while being counted as covering none — and a
> hoisted `init` would count them as GETs.

## MONEY-1238 — the inert-signal wave (a computed verdict must reach a decider)

Seventeen new files, **216 cases**, plus 33 cases added to existing files. Every
assertion in this wave was MUTATION-VERIFIED: the change was reverted with a
match-count assertion, the suite had to go RED, and the file was restored and
compared byte-for-byte. That protocol earned its keep — it caught **nine
vacuous assertions** across the wave, including three of the orchestrator's own,
each of which PASSED against deliberately broken source.

The defect class: a signal that is computed — a counter, a verdict, an `ok`
flag — and then never wired into the thing that decides (exit code, HTTP status,
alert query, job outcome). It is invisible by construction, because every
number in the log still looks healthy.

Six of the eighteen cases are BEHAVIOURAL: the real script is spawned with `gcloud`/`bq`/`curl`/`sleep` stubbed and the assertions read the actual request sequence, which is how the fail-closed and upsert properties are pinned rather than asserted from text. Exactly FOUR IAM roles — a widening to `roles/editor` or `roles/owner` fails, and a whole-file scan rejects any primitive role. Stage 4 is fail-closed on the Detailed Usage Cost BigQuery export (console-only to enable, and it accumulates only from the day it is switched on, so writing a cost config over an empty dataset would look configured and report nothing). Both Datadog writes are GET-then-PATCH/POST upserts, never blind POSTs. And a scan asserts NO `monitor-*.json` and NO dashboard references any `gcp.*` metric yet — MONEY-1238's rule that no monitor may exist over a series nobody has observed arriving; mutation-verified from both directions. **Extended after the first LIVE run (2026-09-11)**: Datadog answers the accounts LIST with **404** when no GCP integration exists — which is the state the very first registration runs in. The script treated every non-2xx as indeterminate and refused, so the one run it exists to perform could never succeed. A PAIR of cases now pins the real rule, DETERMINACY rather than a status code: 404 proceeds to POST, 403 still refuses. The hash is over EVERY contributing file, sorted (walk order is incidental), keyed on GENERATIONS not names (MONEY-1169 rewrote thousands of feed objects IN PLACE) and REFUSING an empty set, because sha256("") is a stable wrong value that would claim a month nothing was read for. A FUTURE stores NULL strike and NULL option type decided on the INSTRUMENT TYPE, never on Mongo's `0`/`"XX"` sentinels — a `0` strike sorts, aggregates and charts as a price, and a future sentinel spelled `"NA"` would leak through a value test. An absent delivery SERIES stays NULL: MTO rows carry no SERIES column at all (per-file-derivable-map.md correction 2) and defaulting to `EQ` fabricates exactly the value a delivery screen must exclude, since BE/BZ is 100% delivery by construction. `expectedSessions` is DATES READ, not trading days — this repo has no calendar reaching 1994, so weekday-counting would make every month with a holiday read partial and the gate would be weakened to `>= 1`. `monthDeleteBounds` rolls the YEAR in December (a bare `month + 1` yields `2024-13-01`, and clamping it deletes nothing) and round-trips against `indiaPartitionKey`, so the rows deleted and the rows loaded are the same month BY CONSTRUCTION. **TWO DEFECTS WERE FOUND BY RE-READING RATHER THAN BY A TEST, and both were made unrepresentable rather than merely fixed.** (a) `decideMonth`'s `expectedSessions` counted FILES, and from 2024 onward two families publish every session of three of the four tables — a healthy 21-session month reads 42 files, `21 >= 42` is false, and `acceptPartition` would have THROWN on every month the replay exists to load. A gate that refuses health is worse than no gate. It takes `ReadonlySet<string>` on both sides now, so a file counter is a type error at the call site. (b) `replaceMonth` scoped its DELETE by `parser_version`, which is in the ledger key precisely so a parser FIX re-runs over unchanged bytes — the rows a reload must remove carry the PREVIOUS version, so the predicate removed nothing and the month held both parses. ## MONEY-1239 — the switchover blocker was DEFINITIONAL, and the gate was hiding it

Adjudicated against **screener.in as a third source**. 3MINDIA reconciles 12/12
to the rupee against screener's CONSOLIDATED while the vendor matches its
STANDALONE — so our arithmetic was never the problem. The two sides differ on
exactly one line item, OTHER INCOME, which the vendor folds into `revenue` (their
column is TOTAL INCOME) and into `operatingIncome` (EBIT INCLUDING other income).

Two things came out of making that visible.

**The gate was already translating silently.** `operatingIncome` reported
"match 112"; with TRANSLATED as its own bucket that is **13 raw matches and 99
translations**. The rates did not move — the change is diagnostic by design — but
the composition was invisible, and a reader could not tell a definitional match
from a real one.

**The gate was compensating for a defect in the writer.** `xbrl-reconcile.ts`
offered `ebitdaRaw - exceptional` as a translation covering 20.1% of surviving
EBITDA disagreements, because `projectFinancials` never removed exceptional items
from EBITDA. BHARTIARTL Q2-FY20: a -30,711 Cr AGR provision turned a +8,928 Cr
EBITDA into -21,783 Cr — a SIGN FLIP feeding `ebitdaMargin` (-103.1%) and
`evToEbitda`. Now removed, guarded per filing: measured on prod over the 4,724
non-banking ANNUAL filings with a material exceptional item, 4,697 satisfy the
signed identity (99.4%), ZERO satisfy the unsigned one, and the 27 that satisfy
neither are left untouched rather than guessed at.

### MONEY-1250 (T3.2 / T3.3) — two gate improvements, both measured on prod first

**T3.2 — a vendor-free, SIBLING-free scale check.** `judgeFilingScale` needs 3+
comparable sibling periods and a period on each side; measured on prod
2026-08-26 under the writer's own nightly scoping, 123 winner periods have ZERO
comparable siblings and 455 have exactly one, so **578 filings it cannot judge
at all**, and its recall over the vendor-visible mismatches is 31% (5 of 16).
`paidUpEquityShareCapital` is the parent's own share capital, so a company's
CONSOLIDATED and STANDALONE filings for one period must state the same number —
an oracle needing no siblings, no ordering and no vendor. 45 ANNUAL + 118
QUARTERLY + 3 HALF_YEARLY (symbol, period) pairs disagree by >= 9.5x with both
sides non-zero. QUARANTINE only: the evidence is symmetric and cannot say which
side is wrong, nor whether the fault is the whole filing (TRENT FY2022, "Lakhs"
vs "Crores") or one mis-tagged element (SHK FY2023, 1,000,006x with both bases
labelled "Crores"), so the verdict carries the sentence saying so.

**T3.3 — the THIRD negated-label shape.** Some filers tag BOTH attribution lines
as unsigned magnitudes of a loss. The existing mask compares `|attributable|`
against `|pfp - nci|`, which is wrong by 2\*nci when the minority line is flipped
too, so it refuses and the projection writes a PROFIT for a loss year. 19 ANNUAL

- 31 QUARTERLY consolidated filings match; 13 + 21 were already handled; 6 + 10
  are new. The tie-break between the two readings is scored on the filing's OWN
  identity residual rather than on branch order — measured, positional precedence
  is wrong in 10 of the 17 overlapping rows.

Every assertion below was mutation-verified (19 mutations, 19 killed, each one
grep-confirmed to have landed before the suite ran).

### A lender does not OWN the columns it cannot source

The founder's call was "do not empty what we cannot fill". The first attempt did
that by keeping the vendor's number when the projection came up empty — it
worked, and it cost: the row was stamped `NSE_XBRL` while two columns were not
ours (the unattributable state MONEY-1175 spent months in), so it also needed an
attribution map, a prior-map merge so a refresh could not relabel the column, and
a rule that UNCHANGED be judged post-patch or the value was re-nulled the next
night. Three mechanisms to make one workaround honest.

The root cause was simpler: `ownedFields` was FAMILY-BLIND, so the writer claimed
`operatingIncome` and `ebitda` for lenders and wrote an explicit NULL whenever
the projection came up empty — which for lenders is almost always
(`operatingProfitBeforeProvisions` is in 76 of 741 ANNUAL banking filings and 0
of 206 NBFC; `ebitda` is REFUSED outright for lenders because interest is their
cost of goods). The module already held the right opinion in two places — it
declines to compute lender EBITDA, and declines to list it in `unfilled` because
"for a bank there is nothing to fill" — and only the ownership list disagreed.

This is the `grossProfit` decision from MONEY-1235 taken one dimension further:
that column left `INCOME_FIELDS` because NO filer can supply it; these two leave
it per FAMILY because lenders cannot. Declaring the column unowned needs no new
machinery — the incumbent survives for the ordinary reason an unowned column
always does, the patch never mentions it — and `source` keeps the meaning it
already had, "the columns we own came from here", exactly as it does for
`grossProfit` and the cash-flow columns.

Stated cost: the 10% of banks whose filings DO carry the RBI line keep the
vendor's number rather than ours. The column still shows a figure, and
consistency about what we source is worth more than one column in ten being
fresher. The gate's own nulling count is now FIELD-aware to match, so it stops
reporting a loss that no longer happens.

Not fixed, deliberately, and recorded on MONEY-1239: a blanket lender
`revenue := totalIncome` was implemented and REVERTED — it fixes Ind-AS
financials like 360ONE and breaks every RBI Form-A bank, and `values` alone
cannot tell the two filing shapes apart because the concept map folds
`InterestEarned` into `revenueFromOperations`. One company is not evidence for a
change to a table with no `source` in its unique key.

## MONEY-1238 batches B-E — the rest of the inert-signal tail

Four parallel agents, **181 mutations between them, every one resolved**. Six
assertions were found VACUOUS and repaired before their results were accepted —
including two where the _mutation_ was the invalid thing, not the test: one
relaxed a guard that `Number.isFinite(null)` already made false, another was a
pure reformat. A survivor is a question, not a verdict.

Three agents corrected the brief they were given, which is the point of asking
them to verify rather than apply: the stated cause for `price-sync` was WRONG
(`yahooFetchQuotes` never rejects — it wraps chunks in `Promise.allSettled` — so
removing the worker's catch would have fixed nothing); `alert-evaluator` has
EIGHT swallows, not seven; `mf-portfolio-sync` had a THIRD unguarded site; and
the screener's `continue`-on-unknown-field is UNREACHABLE today, a latent trap
rather than a live bug.

## Maintenance Rules

> **IMPORTANT:** These rules must be followed whenever tests are modified.

> **Freshness check (the MONEY-838 "durable fix"):**
> `yarn test:coverage-check` (`scripts/gen-test-coverage.ts`) derives the test
> FILE inventory from disk and fails if it differs from the
> "**Total Test Files:** N" headline above. It runs in CI
> (`.github/workflows/test.yml`, warn-only until the next full recount
> restamps the headline). Run it without `--check` for the per-workspace
> report plus a list of files the doc never mentions. Case counts stay
> runtime-derived (`node:test` output) — the script deliberately does not
> guess them statically.

1. **When adding a new test file:**
   - Add it to the appropriate section in this document
   - Update the test case count
   - Move the source file from "Not Tested" to "Tested" if applicable
   - Update the coverage percentage for that area
   - Update the total counts in the Overall Coverage Summary table

2. **When modifying an existing test file:**
   - Update the test case count if `it()` / `test()` calls were added or removed
   - Update the total test case count

3. **When adding a new source file:**
   - Add it to the appropriate "Not Tested" section with a priority
   - Update the source file count in the Overall Coverage Summary

4. **When deleting a test or source file:**
   - Remove the entry from this document
   - Update all affected counts and percentages

5. **Format for test entries:**

   ```
   | `source-file.ts` | `__tests__/category/test-file.test.ts` | <count> | PASS |
   ```

6. **After any update:** Re-run `yarn test` and update the pass rate at the top
   of the file.

7. **Recommended (MONEY-838) — automate this:** these counts are maintained by
   hand and have drifted badly more than once (the headline, the per-PR totals,
   and the two CLAUDE.md files each carried different numbers — 690 vs 674 vs
   271 files; 16,884 vs 22,050/22,164 vs 11,501 cases). The durable fix is a
   `scripts/gen-test-coverage.ts` that runs the suite, reads each file's
   `# tests` (== `it()`/`test()` count), and regenerates the tables + headline —
   wired into CI as a freshness check that fails the PR when this file is stale.
   Until that exists, treat the headline (recounted via `yarn test`) as canonical
   and the per-PR totals below as point-in-time history. The two CLAUDE.md files
   no longer hard-code counts — they point here, so they can't drift again.

### The egress boundary (+2 files / +16 cases) — headline 1226 -> 1228

| File                                            | Cases | What it holds down                                                                                                                     |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ----- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `apps/web/__tests__/meta/no-sec-egress.test.ts` | 8     | apps/web references none of `sec.gov`, `data.sec.gov`, `efts.sec.gov`, `api.openfigi.com`, `edgartools` or `services/us-fundamentals`. |
| `apps/api/__tests__/meta/no-sec-egress.test.ts` | 8     | The same boundary for the mobile API.                                                                                                  |

The `no-feed-fetch-bypass` suite guards the SEAM — a fetch that skips the
archive. These guard the BOUNDARY, and the distinction is the point: SEC's
10 req/s fair-access limit is enforced PER IP, and every Cloud Run service in
this project shares one set of egress addresses. A render path reaching sec.gov
would not merely bypass the archive; it would spend a budget it cannot see,
from a process that has no limiter, once per page view. The remedy for
exceeding it is to stay quiet for ten minutes, and the signal is a 403 with a
BODY rather than a 429 — so it would present as blank fundamentals app-wide
with nothing in the logs naming a rate limit.

Both strip comments first (a file explaining that it deliberately does NOT call
SEC must not be a violation — that is how a guard gets deleted rather than
fixed), both assert the scan actually walked the app (a scan that silently
reads nothing passes every assertion), and both carry a non-vacuity case
driving the predicate over a synthetic file, because the real set is empty by
design. Mutation-verified by adding a genuine `fetch("https://data.sec.gov/...")`
to `apps/web/lib` and an OpenFIGI call to `apps/api/src`: both named the file.

`FEED_HOSTS` also gained `data.sec.gov`, `efts.sec.gov` and `api.openfigi.com`.
That tripped the suite's own no-stale-entries rule, which requires every listed
host to appear in `packages/core/src` — and OpenFIGI's only caller is Python.
Rather than drop the entry (which would remove the protection that makes a
FUTURE TypeScript fetch fail), the invariant was kept and its scope widened:
`NON_TS_FEED_HOSTS` records such hosts with a written reason, and a new
assertion checks each one still appears in `services/`, walking `.py` with its
own walker — the shared `walk()` filters on SOURCE_EXT and would have returned
an empty string that passed.

### The schema parity guard (+1 file / +10 cases) — headline 1228 -> 1229

| File                                                            | Cases | What it holds down                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | ----- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `packages/core/__tests__/us-fundamentals/schema-parity.test.ts` | 20    | Prisma's eleven `us_*` models and the Python row models that write them describe the SAME document — field for field, in both directions. **10 -> 13**: names were only half the contract. Types are now compared too (`Int` vs `str` is a read-time conversion error on rows that were written happily), and nullability in the direction that breaks: `to_doc()` OMITS a `None`, so a Python-optional field against a Prisma-REQUIRED column writes a document with the key missing. Types come from `models.py` parsed as TEXT — the committed snapshot is names-only by construction — with a premise case asserting the text parse finds exactly the snapshot's field set. What it deliberately does NOT cover is written down in the file: `Json` is not narrowed (its cell takes a scalar or an array, and `UsFundamentals.asReported` is `Json` against a Python `list[dict]` today), numeric width, value domains, and defaults. |

There is no ORM between the two sides: pymongo writes the key the Python model
spelled and Prisma reads the key it declared, so a misspelling raises nothing
anywhere. Prisma-only fields become columns that are ALWAYS ABSENT — and on
Mongo absent is not null, so `{f: null}` and `{f: {not: null}}` both return zero
rows, which is the confusion behind MONEY-1050/1234/1235/1236. Python-only
fields become undeclared attributes with no index, which work until the first
query that needs one.

The comparison drops `id` from the Prisma side (`@map("_id")` — MongoDB owns
it), and a dedicated case asserts every model still DECLARES `id`, so the
exemption cannot start hiding a genuinely missing column. It also checks each
`@@map` against `collections.py` in both directions: a `@@map` the Python side
does not name is unreachable (`collection_name()` raises), and a name with no
`@@map` creates a real collection with no schema, no indexes and no entry in the
prod->QA sync.

Three of the ten are premise cases, because a parse that silently yields nothing
would make the rest a comparison of two empty sets: the block must yield exactly
the eleven models BY NAME, every line inside them must parse as a comment, a
block attribute or a field (a line the parser drops disappears from the Prisma
side and then reports as a Python-only field, pointing at the wrong file), and
`collections.py` must yield eleven plain-literal entries.

The last two cases guard the SNAPSHOT ITSELF. This test reads
`services/us-fundamentals/tests/_schema_snapshot.json`, which
`test_store_models.py` generates and commits — read here so the guard runs in
the TypeScript build with no interpreter present, since `services/` is outside
the Yarn workspace globs and cannot be imported. A generated file that is read
but never regenerated rots in place while everything above it stays green, so
the snapshot's model names are also compared against the `MODELS` registry
parsed out of `models.py` as TEXT, and every `Row` subclass declared there must
be registered in it — an unregistered row model is invisible to
`schema_snapshot()` and therefore to this entire file. A missing snapshot FAILS
with "re-run `yarn test:python`"; it never skips.

Nine mutations run, each confirmed red then restored byte-identically
(checksummed): a Prisma field deleted (`UsFundamentals.isLatest`) and a Prisma
field added (`UsFiler.legalDomicile`) — the two directions are separate code
paths and each was driven; a model deleted from the snapshot; a bogus twelfth
model added to the snapshot; the snapshot moved aside (red with the regenerate
message, `# skipped 0`); a collection renamed in `collections.py` (red in BOTH
directions, each naming its own remedy); a row model unregistered from `MODELS`;
a Prisma model renamed; `id` dropped from `UsEdgarCursor` (which the field
comparison CANNOT see, since `id` is exempt from it — that mutation is the only
evidence the `id` case is load-bearing); and an unparseable Prisma line
(`@unique` on its own line) to prove the premise case fires instead of
misattributing the loss to Python.

Every assertion was mutation-verified: 15 mutations in round 1, 14 more in round
2, each producing exactly the expected red, then restored. The behavioural cases
are now IN the file rather than run beside it: `runLadder` executes the real
`setup-infra.sh` / `setup-pubsub.sh` with `gcloud` stubbed by a bash FUNCTION
sourced through `BASH_ENV` — not an EXPORTED function, because bash 3.2 (what
macOS ships) CLEARS `BASH_SOURCE` when a shell calls a function imported from
the environment, which kills any script reading `${BASH_SOURCE[0]}` after its
first stubbed call. `PATH` is also REPLACED with a deny-shim ahead of
`/usr/bin`, so a harness whose `BASH_ENV` fails to load reaches a loud 127
rather than real infrastructure, and every case asserts the call log is
non-empty and free of `PATH-STUB-REACHED` before it grades an exit code.

### dist-clean vs a submodule (+1 file) — headline 1237 -> 1238

| File                                             | Cases | What it holds down                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ----- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `packages/core/__tests__/ops/dist-clean.test.ts` | 4     | That `dist-clean` skips git-tracked `dist/` artefacts INCLUDING ones inside a submodule. The guard asked the SUPERPROJECT's index — `git ls-files vendor/charting_library/datafeeds/udf/dist/bundle.js` answers "did not match any file(s) known to git" for a file the submodule tracks perfectly well — so it read "untracked" and every `yarn build` deleted it. That is why `vendor/charting_library` showed as permanently modified: not a stray local edit, the build doing it each time. It also made the verify-gate's tree hash depend on whether a build had run since the marker was written, which blocked a gated remote update with a content-changed error `git status` could not explain. Fixed with `git -C "$rel" ls-files .`, which resolves to whichever repo owns the directory. Carries a PREMISE case (the bundle exists and the submodule tracks it, so the assertions cannot pass against an absent directory) and a REGRESSION case pinning that the superproject alone still sees zero — if that ever changes, the guard's reasoning needs re-checking rather than silently over-matching. |

### CI shell portability (+1 file) — headline 1238 -> 1239

| File                                                          | Cases | What it holds down                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ----- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `packages/core/__tests__/ops/shell-script-invocation.test.ts` | 4     | That a script's INTERPRETER matches what the script uses. `package.json` ran `sh scripts/run-python-tests.sh`, and an explicit interpreter OVERRIDES the shebang — so the file's own `#!/usr/bin/env bash` was ignored. macOS `/bin/sh` is bash in POSIX mode and accepts `set -o pipefail`; CI's is dash, which answers `Illegal option -o pipefail` and exits 2. The whole Python suite (1,414 cases) never ran, and because the failure was in the SHELL nothing about the tests looked wrong. **The local verify gate cannot catch this class** — the developer machine only reproduces it by invoking dash explicitly, which is why it is a test and not vigilance. Checks both directions: a bash-shebang script is never invoked with `sh`, and a script invoked with `sh` contains no bashisms (so a POSIX file that later grows one is caught before CI). Found a SECOND live instance on its first run — `scripts/ops/dist-clean.sh`, same shebang, same `pipefail`, same `sh` invocation — verified broken under dash and fixed with it. |

### MONEY-1276: a null inside SEC's arrays (Python only — headline unchanged)

`tests/test_edgar_adapter.py` (+5 cases). `edgar-bulk-submissions-prod` failed on
its first production run: a filer in `submissions.zip` carries
`exchanges: [null]`, the adapter passed the array through verbatim, and
`UsFilerRow.exchangesAsFiled` is `list[str]` — so pydantic refused the row and
ONE bad filer aborted the entire run.

The strict model is not the defect; it is what surfaced this rather than letting
`None` into a column every reader would have to guard. The fix drops nulls at
the BOUNDARY (`_clean_str_tuple`), applied to `exchanges` and `tickers` alike.
The fifth case asserts the row model still REFUSES a null if the boundary is
bypassed — so the strictness that caught this cannot be relaxed as the "fix".

### The Python suite is deliberately NOT in the headline

`services/us-fundamentals` holds **1,392 pytest cases** (measured
2026-08-29 with `python -m pytest -q`; 2 skipped) across ~55 files, plus 15
captured SEC fixtures. The figure here read "~305" for several rounds while the
suite more than quadrupled — a hand-maintained count with no generator behind
it, which is the same drift `**Total Test Files:**` exists to catch on the
TypeScript side. Re-measure rather than trusting this line.

They are not counted here because `scripts/gen-test-coverage.ts` matches
`/\.test\.tsx?$/` across `apps/*`, `packages/*` and `workers` — a Python
directory is in none of those, by construction: `services/` sits outside the
Yarn workspace globs precisely so turbo, tsc and this generator do not walk it.
Bumping the headline for them would make the count disagree with the inventory
the script measures, which is the one thing the `--check` gate exists to stop.

They ARE gated, in both places that matter: `.github/workflows/test.yml` runs a
`yarn test:python` job (with a redis service, so the fair-access load test is
real rather than self-skipped), and `.claude/hooks/run-verify.sh` runs the same
script as phase [2/5]. `apps/web/__tests__/ci/verify-gate-parity.test.ts`
asserts those two stay in step.

### MONEY-1279 / MONEY-1280: a holiday is not a 404 (Python only — headline unchanged)

`tests/test_client.py` **41 -> 45**, `tests/test_ownership_backfill.py`
**20 -> 27**, `tests/test_xbrl_backfill.py` **25 -> 26**. No new files, so the
headline does not move.

The first production 5-year ownership backfill died 33 minutes in on
`daily-index/2021/QTR3/form.20210906.idx` — **Labor Day**. Measured with the
job's own User-Agent, 09-03 and 09-07 answer 200 and only the holiday 403s, so
it was never a block on our egress: sec.gov's archive bucket denies
`ListBucket`, and S3 will not confirm an absence it has not authorised you to
observe, so a key that does not exist answers `AccessDenied` rather than
`NoSuchKey`.

`ownership_backfill.py` already had a correct, carefully-argued `NO_INDEX` /
`CHECKPOINT_EMPTY` branch for exactly this case. It was reachable only from a
404, so it was **structurally unreachable for the case it was written for**, and
~50 holidays sit in a 5-year window.

**Why the suite was green over it.** The existing
`test_a_day_with_no_index_file_is_named_and_is_not_a_failure` drives a
`RecordingIndexFetcher` that returns `None` from a dict. It pins the BRANCH and
is correct — but it injects the very absence under test, so it can say nothing
about whether anything ever reaches that branch, and `default_fetch_index` had
no coverage at all. The new `test_THE_JOIN_a_holiday_403_becomes_None_...`
drives the real function through the real classification table; its companions
assert a rate block and an unclassifiable 403 still PROPAGATE, which is the
property that makes mapping any 403 to "SEC published nothing that day" safe.
Ordering is the whole safety argument, so `ARCHIVE_ABSENT_MARKERS` is tested
LAST, after both block markers, and a body carrying both still classifies as the
block.

The second defect surfaced from the same incident: the run had walked five days
and left **zero** checkpoints. Checkpoints flushed only at
`writers.DEFAULT_CHUNK` (500) or after a clean exit, and a 23h budget covers
~300 days — so the in-loop flush was unreachable and an exception skipped the
trailing one. Both are fixed (`CHECKPOINT_FLUSH_DAYS = 10`, trailing flush in a
`finally`), and BOTH are pinned: one case on the constant, and a behavioural one
driving the call site, because restoring `DEFAULT_CHUNK` there leaves the
constant assertion green while making the flush dead code again — the same
"pins construction, not use" shape that let the original through.
`xbrl_backfill.py` carried the identical unprotected trailing flush (bounded,
since its chunk is over filings where 500 is reachable) and gets the same
`finally` and its own abort test.

All seven mutations verified red: removing the archive check, checking it before
the block markers, dropping the `SecNotFound` subclassing, restoring
`DEFAULT_CHUNK` at the call site, removing either `finally`, and narrowing the
`except` back to a literal 404.

### MONEY-1281 / MONEY-1282: newest-first walks, and news is not a market (Python + TS, headline unchanged)

No new test files, and no net case change — four existing cases were rewritten
against a changed contract, which is the interesting part.

`walk_days` yielded ASCENDING, so every backfill filled history from the least
useful end. Measured mid-walk on prod, `us_insider_transactions` held **12,897
rows for 2021 and 47 for 2025** — a five-year walk had spent its first runs on
the year nobody queries and was still days from the years everyone does. A long
backfill is N budget-limited runs that get READ between them, so run one should
leave the most-asked-about year complete.

The ordering is free to change because it carries no correctness weight:
checkpoints are keyed per DAY and `load_checkpoints` returns them as a set, so
resume is order-independent.

**Four cases failed on the change, which is the evidence they were not vacuous.**
They were genuinely pinning ascending order rather than merely passing:

- `test_the_walk_is_inclusive_ascending_and_refuses_an_inverted_window` becomes
  `..._NEWEST_FIRST_...` and now asserts BOTH directions, plus the property that
  matters most here: an inverted window stays a `ValueError` in both modes. A
  reversed walk is exactly what an inverted window now resembles, and silently
  reinterpreting it as one would turn a caller's bug into plausible output.
- `test_a_day_with_no_index_file_is_named_and_is_not_a_failure` and
  `test_the_budget_stops_between_days_and_reports_resumable` — day-order and
  checkpoint expectations inverted.
- `test_a_run_that_ABORTS_still_records_the_days_it_FINISHED` now explodes on the
  OLDEST day, because that is the one walked LAST.

`news-sync-market-hours` ran `* * 1-5`, so weekend news was never fetched:
`stock_news` sat 43.6h stale on a Sunday while `news_articles` (RSS, every 15
minutes, all week) was 15.6h. The two feeds had diverged by a day and a half
with nothing erroring. Before changing the schedule, the worker was checked for
an internal weekday gate — there is none, only a stale comment — because a
scheduler change buys nothing if the job gates too, and that one-fact-two-sources
shape is what hid `MF_METADATA_PROVIDER` for months.

### MONEY-1283…1291: the data-engine audit wave (+4 files — headline 1239 -> 1243)

Four new TypeScript test files, and +37 Python cases across six existing ones
(1,437 -> 1,474). Python per-file after the wave: `test_bulk_common.py` 50,
`test_bulk_companyfacts.py` 60, `test_bulk_submissions.py` 30, `test_client.py`
45, `test_backfill_logic.py` 49, `test_ownership_backfill.py` 27.

| new file                                                                | cases | pins                                                                                                                       |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `packages/core/__tests__/market-data/reconcile-symbol-paging.test.ts`   | 12    | the F3 gate reads in symbol pages, and `main()` goes THROUGH the pager                                                     |
| `workers/__tests__/processors/xbrl-ratios-arm.test.ts`                  | 17    | `XBRL_RATIOS_APPLY` arms ratios while `XBRL_PROJECTION_APPLY` still gates the projection; both flags PRESENT in both specs |
| `workers/__tests__/processors/bse-announcements-sync-drain.test.ts`     | 15    | the retry arm, category round-robin, and ONE follow-up per chain link                                                      |
| `workers/__tests__/processors/us-eod-sync-permaticker-prefetch.test.ts` | 7     | an unkeyable fund is never FETCHED, only skipped                                                                           |

**The recurring lesson across all four, and it is the same one every time.** A
test that drives the new unit directly cannot tell a wired fix from a disarmed
one. Three of these files carry an explicit WIRING assertion beside the
behavioural ones, and in every case the wiring mutation was the one that
survived the behavioural suite:

- reconcile: pointing `main()` back at a bare `findMany` left all 12 behavioural
  cases GREEN and reddened only the two wiring assertions. An exported pager
  nothing calls is a fix that ships disarmed.
- ratios: `xbrl-ratios-wired.test.ts` now asserts the processor mentions the OLD
  flag NOWHERE, so the split cannot silently become additive.
- BSE: "exactly ONE follow-up per run" — moving the publish per-item reddens 5.
- fund NAV: the assertion is a NEGATIVE (a call NOT made), which is why the
  price-leg collaborators had to become an injectable seam; two further guards
  assert the injected defaults ARE the production collaborators, so the seam
  cannot quietly become a test-only path.

**Two fixture limitations recorded in the tests rather than left implicit.**
`FakeDatabase` is an in-memory dict and does not encode BSON, so it can never
reproduce pymongo's `OverflowError` — the MONEY-1284 sanitiser test therefore
pins the COERCION, and the raise path is covered separately by injecting the
exception. And the MONEY-1283 read-count assertion counts member reads BY NAME
rather than wall time, because a timing assertion passes trivially against the
local `zip_from_bytes` fixture while production stays network-bound — which is
exactly the gap that hid the defect.

### MONEY-1293 / 1299 / 1302 / 1303: group C (+3 files — headline 1243 -> 1246)

| new file                                                                  | cases | pins                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `workers/__tests__/processors/xbrl-sync-instrument-rung.test.ts`          | 14    | the ISIN candidate order is TOTAL, so two runs cannot attach a filing to different listings       |
| `workers/__tests__/processors/news-sync-population-and-rotation.test.ts`  | 16    | constituents are their own OR arm; the stamp is exchange-scoped; rotation still stamps on FAILURE |
| `packages/core/__tests__/market-data/sector-taxonomy-write-guard.test.ts` | 14    | every live sector writer refuses a non-canonical value                                            |

Plus +10 Python cases for `NO_PARSER` (1,474 -> 1,481), and 3 cases added to
`schema-parity.test.ts` (20 -> 23), and `monitor-agreement.test.ts` 31 -> 40.

**Three of these tickets began by falsifying their own premise, and the tests
exist because of what the measurement found, not what the ticket asked for.**

- MONEY-1299 was written as "the ISIN join is too narrow". Buckets (a) and (c)
  measured ZERO — the join was never filtered — so the proposed fix recovered
  nothing. The same query found an unordered `findFirst` attaching **78.3% of
  filings to the wrong exchange's listing**, invisible because it mints a second
  row rather than colliding. The 14 cases pin the ORDER, which is what was
  actually broken.
- MONEY-1302 was written as "101 rows need aliases". 58 were already aliased,
  and **57 of the 101 are bonds wearing `instrumentType: "EQUITY"`** — so
  mapping `Other` to the empty `Diversified` bucket, the obvious move, would
  have handed 26 debt instruments a sector chip. The write guard is the durable
  half, and the sweep found a SECOND unguarded writer the ticket never mentioned.
- MONEY-1303 asserted `schema-parity.test.ts` "will demand both sides". It does
  not — it compares names and types, never values, and the status vocabulary
  lived in a `///` comment nothing read. Proven by running that mutation FIRST
  and watching the file pass 20/20 with the new status on one side only.

**A fixture supplied the property one test claimed to verify.** In
`news-sync-population-and-rotation`, flipping the rotation `asc -> desc`
initially stayed GREEN: the fake sorted stale-first unconditionally and ignored
the caller's `orderBy`. The fake now honours direction, the baseline was
retaken, and the affected mutations were re-run against it. This is the third
distinct instance in this wave of a test passing for a reason other than the one
claimed — see also the `FakeDatabase`/BSON and read-count-vs-wall-time notes
above.

### MONEY-1298 / 1301: group D (+2 files — headline 1246 -> 1248)

| new file                                                                     | cases | pins                                                                                 |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `packages/core/__tests__/market-data/instrument-classification-1298.test.ts` | 36    | every retype rule needs a POSITIVE feed signal; ISIN-absence alone never types a row |
| `workers/__tests__/processors/corporate-actions-isin-join.test.ts`           | 15    | the ISIN join keys on (symbol, exchange) TOGETHER, and refuses rather than guessing  |

**A discriminator validated on the rows it was DERIVED from was wrong on the rows
it would ACT on.** MONEY-1302 characterised 30 NHAI bonds as "BSE group still
stamped `EQ`, no ISIN" and that was correct for those 30. Measured against the
whole 5,392-row population that rule selects, it also contains **~45 real
companies** (TEMPSENS, NOVYRA PHARMACHEM, AUGMONT, BENARA BEARINGS), ~45 MF
plans and ~55 index rows — all of which it would have typed DEBT, removing them
from the screener with no re-enrichment path back. "No ISIN implies not equity"
is separately falsified by AUGMONT, a real newly-listed company that simply has
none yet.

Every rule therefore requires a positive signal from the feed, with ISIN-absence
demoted to a gate. Mutation M5 restores the old shape and reddens on exactly the
companies it would have mistyped.

**Two guards proved themselves at runtime rather than in a fixture.** The
retype script's write guard was counted against prod: `isin` absent on 7,285
active NSE rows, bare-null on **zero** — so without its `isSet` arm the guard
would have matched nothing and the entire NSE half of `--apply` would have
written 0 rows and reported success. And before proposing anything for the ~870
suffixed twins, `daily_prices` was checked: 13,917 rows are keyed to the
suffixed `_id` across 446 twins, and `DailyPrice.instrumentId` is a REQUIRED
relation, so deactivating them would throw and blank every result that touches
one.

**A fixture reached only half its rule.** Mutation M6 initially survived because
the test used a `-N1` symbol, which exercises only the series FAMILY arm; the
EXACT arm was untested. A `-SG` case now covers it and both mutations are red.
That is the fourth instance in this wave of a test passing for a reason other
than the one claimed.

### MONEY-1300 step 3: the basis a figure is on (+3 files)

Step 2's own suite — `packages/core/__tests__/market-data/financials-basis-backfill.test.ts`, the vendor-row stamp — is the fourth
MONEY-1300 file and is listed in the table above. The headline moves
1248 -> 1252 for the four together.

| new file                                                                 | cases | pins                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `packages/core/__tests__/market-data/financials-basis.test.ts`           | 10    | ABSENT and "UNKNOWN" collapse to one state, and that state is never CONSOLIDATED          |
| `packages/research/__tests__/money1300-financials-basis.test.ts`         | 9     | all three statement tools state a basis on every path, including the ones that have none  |
| `apps/web/__tests__/components/money1300-financials-basis-badge.test.ts` | 8     | the tab renders the badge and the per-column note; TTM's shadowing tooltip carries it too |

**A correct number that cannot be attributed.** An Indian company files the SAME
period twice under SEBI/Ind AS — CONSOLIDATED (parent + subsidiaries) and
STANDALONE (parent alone) — and for a holding company they differ by a MULTIPLE:
360ONE FY2025 `totalAssets` is 19,768 Cr consolidated against 7,332 Cr
standalone. Measured on prod 2026-08-31, 1,786 of 2,467 symbols with an annual
period (72%) file BOTH, 664 standalone only, 17 consolidated only.
`StockFinancials` deliberately keeps ONE row per period, so every reader was
rendering a figure it could not attribute.

**The column was READ and then thrown away.** `getOrFetchFinancials` runs a
`findMany` with NO `select:`, so Prisma already handed `rowToStatement` the whole
document — but the mapper's allowlist copied `period`, `endDate` and the numeric
columns and nothing else. The web and services readers had the opposite defect:
a hardcoded `select:` that omitted `basis`, which is the "we never asked" printing
as "the row has no value" class the F3 reconcile gate hit. Neither is visible from
the output, because an absent field and an unpopulated one render identically.

**The interesting assertion is the one equality cannot make.** ABSENT (the
~32,359 rows a Mongo `db push` never created the field on) and the literal
`"UNKNOWN"` (vendor rows) must render the SAME — and an implementation that
returned `"CONSOLIDATED"` for BOTH satisfies that equality while being exactly
the failure the ticket exists to prevent. Every suite therefore asserts
`notEqual(..., "CONSOLIDATED")` separately. Mutation I flips
`normalizeStockFinancialsBasis`'s absent branch to `"CONSOLIDATED"` and reddens
all three describes in the core suite.

Nine mutations were run in total, one per surface: deleting the mapper line
(reddens the research reader's own suite in apps/web), removing `basis:
UNSTATED_BASIS` from each of the three Yahoo mappers, dropping `metadata.basis`,
removing `basis: true` from each of the two `select:` blocks, deleting the JSX
badge, and the absent-defaults-to-consolidated flip above. All nine reddened.
