## MONEY-1309 T7 — the realtime/news INFRA seams (+1 file / +21 cases)

| File                                                        | Cases | What it holds down                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ----- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `packages/core/__tests__/ops/tiingo-realtime-infra.test.ts` | 32    | Four provisioning files that nothing compiles together. (1) THE AGREEMENT: the raw-tick prefix is stated as a lifecycle `matchesPrefix` in `gcs-lifecycle.json` and as an rsync `--exclude` REGEX in `sync-prod-to-qa.sh`, and the two strings are NOT equal (one is absolute from the bucket root, the other RELATIVE to the rsync SOURCE), so no grep can keep them in step — the test reconstructs one from the other. (2) EVERY non-comment `gcloud storage rsync` line must expand the same exclusion array, dry-run echo included. (3) The applier's guard is EXECUTED. (4) The news poll's cron, prod-only membership, topic and description cap. Its `--tier` usage line now lists `lake` (MONEY-1610); count unchanged — the 21 here was stale, the file ran 32 at HEAD. |

**The guard is RUN, not grepped, and that is the point.** Every other ops test in
this repo reads shell as TEXT, because a shell script's whole output is a
`gcloud` call and `gcloud` is what a test must not run.
`setup-gcs-lifecycle.sh` is the exception worth taking: its refusal logic is a
self-contained `node -e` program that takes its inputs from ENV plus a file and
writes a merged policy, issuing no gcloud call of its own. So the test lifts it
out of the shell source and runs it against synthetic policies, and "a `feeds/`
delete is refused" becomes an observed exit code. A text-match version was
written first and thrown away: it stayed green against a guard whose `every` had
been changed to `some`, because the `REFUSE:` string was still in the file.

Extraction is guarded by a marker floor (`const isOwned`, `const sweeps`,
both env names, the final `process.exit`), so a regex that grabbed the wrong
span cannot quietly "run" something else. It also enforces a constraint on the
SCRIPT: the JS is inside a single-quoted shell string, so it may never contain
an apostrophe.

**Nine mutations, and one of them found a real gap.**

| Mutation                                                       | Reddened                                                                            |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| lifecycle prefix `feeds/TIINGO/ws/` -> `feeds/`                | 7 cases, incl. the agreement and `[premise] it ACCEPTS the policy we actually ship` |
| rsync exclusion `^TIINGO/ws/` -> `^TIINGO/`                    | the agreement case only                                                             |
| exclusion dropped from the REAL call, kept in the dry-run echo | `the exclusion is applied at EVERY rsync site`                                      |
| LOCK 2 sweep test INVERTED                                     | `Delete @ edgar/` + the premise (an over-strict guard is caught too)                |
| LOCK 2 neutered (`if (false && …)`)                            | `Delete @ edgar/`, `LOCK 2 survives a WIDENED allow-list`                           |
| `feeds/` removed from `PROTECTED_ROOTS`                        | 4 cases — the guard's own floor refuses, i.e. it fails CLOSED                       |
| `isOwned` `every` -> `some`                                    | **NOTHING, at first.** See below.                                                   |
| news-poll cron `*/2 * * * *` -> `*/2 * * * 2-6`                | `every 2 minutes, on ALL SEVEN DAYS`                                                |
| topic removed from `BASE_WORKER_TOPICS` only                   | `the topic is created AND given a push subscription`                                |

`every` -> `some` passed 46/46. `matchesPrefix` is a LIST and every case in the
file used a single-prefix rule, which makes the two quantifiers
indistinguishable — the assertions were all true of a guard that would accept a
rule carrying one allow-listed prefix beside `candles/`. A case was added for
exactly that (`SetStorageClass`, not `Delete`, so LOCK 2 cannot catch it by
accident and the case proves something about LOCK 1); it now reddens alone.

**A latent defect fixed on the way in.** `Delete @ edgar/` was allow-listed —
`"edgar/".startsWith("edgar/")` — and INVISIBLE to the pre-existing
"edgar/filings must never be deleted" assertion, which looks for a prefix
STARTING WITH `edgar/filings/`. It would have deleted the permanent SEC archive.
`PROTECTED_ROOTS` holding `edgar/filings/` closes it, and
`edgar-infra-coverage.test.ts` gained a `no Delete rule can sweep a protected
root` case (22 -> 26 cases there; its lifecycle policy path also moves to the
renamed `scripts/ops/gcs-lifecycle.json`).

## MONEY-1346 — ratios for the 1,248 symbols that have NO XBRL FILING

Measured on prod 2026-09-05: **1,248 Indian symbols hold `EXTRACTED` ANNUAL rows
in `document_financial_extracts`, hold no XBRL filing, and hold ZERO
`stock_ratios` rows.** The only live producer selected its candidates with
`xbrlFilings: { some: {} }`, so those companies were never written and never
CONSIDERED — no P/E, no ROE, no margin, and no counter naming the shortfall.

`+37` cases across two NEW files and one WIDENED one.

| file                                                                | cases   | pins                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `packages/core/__tests__/market-data/document-ratio-inputs.test.ts` | 23 NEW  | the CRORES→RUPEES boundary, the three columns that must NOT be scaled, absence-is-never-zero, the fiscal span, and CONSOLIDATED-preferred period selection |
| `workers/__tests__/processors/xbrl-ratios-doc-fallback.test.ts`     | 17 NEW  | the fallback's population, ordering, authority, no-TTM and its own arm flag — the real processor against an in-memory store                                |
| `packages/core/__tests__/market-data/xbrl-ratios-producer.test.ts`  | 36 → 42 | +6: the GLAXO byte-identity baseline across the `RatioInputs` widening                                                                                     |
| `workers/__tests__/processors/xbrl-ratios-arm.test.ts`              | 17      | unchanged count; `DOC_RATIOS_APPLY` added to `INTENDED_FLAG_STATE`, and the derived-flag regex de-scoped from `XBRL_`                                      |

**The GLAXO identity is the load-bearing one.** `projectFinancials`,
`deriveRatios` and `deriveShareCount` were widened from `XbrlFinancials` to a
new `RatioInputs` slice, and two `reportedIncome` FALLBACKS were added inside
them. That is a change to the path EVERY filer flows through, into a table whose
unique key carries no `source`. The baseline in the test was captured by running
the pipeline BEFORE the refactor and diffing after — sha256 `b9d3046…` on both
sides, byte-identical — so the guarantee is "nothing moved", not "the fields
somebody thought to name did not move".

**Seven mutations, and two of them exposed a real defect in the tests or the
source.**

| Mutation                                                                   | Reddened                                                                    |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| drop the `documentFinancialExtracts` arm from the candidate `OR`           | **NOTHING, at first.** See below. After the fix: 10 of 14 cases             |
| `if (recentFilings.length === 0)` → always try extracts first              | `an instrument WITH a filing never issues the extract query`                |
| `env.DOC_RATIOS_APPLY === "true"` → `Boolean(env.DOC_RATIOS_APPLY)`        | the arm suite's deploy contract AND 2 fallback cases                        |
| `RatioInputs` drops `basis` (simulated at the `isAdjacentAnnual` call)     | 3 GLAXO identity cases — `returnBasis` silently flips `AVERAGE` → `CLOSING` |
| `croresToRupees` returns the value unscaled                                | 3 mapper cases + the BSE end-to-end value case                              |
| the fallback's authority guard names `"NSE_XBRL"` instead of `SOURCE`      | `DOC_PDF may not overwrite an NSE_XBRL row`                                 |
| `reportedIncome` promoted from a FALLBACK to an OVERRIDE in `deriveRatios` | **NOTHING** — and that is the correct answer; see below                     |

**The candidate-`OR` mutation survived 14/14 on the first attempt**, which is
the whole reason this ticket exists restated as a test defect: the fake
`instrumentMapping.findMany` returned the instrument unconditionally, so it
could not see a `where` that no longer selected the cohort. Every value
assertion stayed green while the 1,248 symbols were unreachable again. The fake
now EVALUATES the `OR` against the store, and the mutation reddens 10 cases.

**The override mutation reddening nothing is a PROOF, not a gap.** For a
non-lender, `projectFinancials` builds `ebitdaBeforeExceptionalItems` as
`sumAll([pbt, financeCosts, depreciation]) − exceptionalAdjustment(v)` and
`deriveRatios` builds `(pbt + financeCosts − exceptional) + depreciation` — the
same three terms, the same adjustment, refused under the same
`isLenderFamily` predicate. The two are defined together and undefined together
for anything parsed out of a filing, so the `??` is unreachable for every XBRL
caller by construction rather than by hope. That is exactly the property the
fallback needed in order to be safe to add to a one-way-door write path, and the
mutation measures it.

**A latent defect fixed on the way in.** The fallback's authority guard drifted
625 characters away from its `stockRatios.upsert` (a long provenance comment sat
between them), which reddened `financials-write-authority.test.ts` and
`xbrl-ratios-wired.test.ts`'s `the cursor-only stamp sits BEHIND the same
authority guard as the write`. Both scans are enforcing the rule this file's own
comments state — a guard the next edit can separate from its write protects
nothing — and both caught it before the code was ever run.

**And one deploy-spec constraint.** Adding `DOC_RATIOS_APPLY` to both
cloudbuild specs took prod's inline Cloud Run argument to 673 characters of
headroom against `cloudbuild-arg-limit.test.ts`'s 700-character floor — the
guard doing exactly what it exists for, well before the 10,000-character wall
that would fail a release mid-deploy. Bought back the way that test's own
doctrine says: two redundant `# MONEY-980 …` signposts were relocated OUT of the
heredoc (their real content already sits in the outer preamble, which costs
nothing), leaving 804 / 826 characters.

**One source bug the new tests found.** `periodFor` computed a QUARTERLY span by
subtracting three months and then adding a day, which for a 30-June quarter end
yields a start of **31-March** — the last day of the previous quarter, with a
92-day span that still reads like a quarter. The order is now "step to the day
AFTER the end, THEN subtract the span", so the intermediate date is always the
first of a month and can neither clamp nor drift.

| `packages/core/src/ops/lake-release-logic.ts` — B7 (MONEY-1518): immutable, versioned parquet releases + the DuckDB read path. **The ticket's premise was FALSIFIED by measurement and the conversion was NOT done.** Real prod `candles/US/M1/AAPL/{2024,2025}` objects, decoded and re-encoded through `encodeColdShard` itself (round-trip byte-exact against stored): 123,072 rows = 1,912,970 B JSONL_GZ vs 2,364,453 B parquet, **+23.6%**; 125,527 rows **+22.9%**. The overhead amortises from D1's +68% but **never crosses zero**, and it is NOT monotonic — the same bars truncated give +93.2% @252, +21.6% @5k, +8.5% @20k, +7.1% @50k and back to **+25.3% @100k**, so a row-group boundary makes a BIGGER shard worse. Do not convert the cold store at any timeframe. What parquet is for here is the RELEASE artifact, which is a different object with a different job. A release is `releases/{release_id}/` where the id IS the snapshot instant — one clock, not two; colon-free so it survives a shell arg; sorts lexically so `latest_release()` is `max()`. **Readers MUST pin**: every entry point requires `release`, there is no default and no implicit newest. Immutability is BigQuery's own — `EXPORT DATA ... overwrite = false` fails on an existing object, because a read-then-write would race a retried job against itself. `EXPORT DATA` and not `bq extract`, since `adjusted_bar_d1` is a VIEW and extract jobs refuse views. Checksums are `crc32c` in a NAMED `{algo, value}` field — GCS populates it on every object at zero cost, where sha256 would mean re-downloading a multi-GB release per cut. **Mutation-verified 22/22** across TS and Python, and three SOURCE defects were found while writing the tests: `releaseId` let `toISOString` throw a bare `RangeError` BEFORE its own Invalid-Date guard; `releaseKey` accepted a whitespace-only relPath (GCS will store an object literally named `"   "`); and `lake.bars` resolved `LAKE_ENV` before validating its own `release` argument, so a bad release on a shell without `LAKE_ENV` blamed the environment                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | `packages/core/__tests__/ops/lake-release-logic.test.ts`                           | 49         | PASS   |

Also scans the job: it uses `listObjects` (THROWS) never `listFiles` (returns `[]`), refuses an empty listing rather than reporting a clean run, never claims MISSING (no vendor manifest proves a loss here, unlike Databento) and stamps `acquired_at` from the EX-DATE, not the run clock — it is the PARTITION column. Mutation-verified four ways.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | `packages/core/__tests__/market-data/tiingo-corp-actions-ledger.test.ts`           | 19         | PASS   |
| `packages/core/src/market-data/intraday/rollup-logic.ts` (A5, MONEY-1470) — the ring buffer's rules, and the file that caught `rollUp` fabricating bars. It returned its input UNCHANGED whenever the target was 1m, so a 5-minute India buffer answered a 1-minute request with five-minute bars LABELLED as one-minute — each plotting at a real minute with an OHLC describing four minutes it does not claim, undetectable downstream. `IntervalNotDerivableError` now refuses any target that is not a whole multiple of the base, and the refusal fires on an EMPTY buffer too, so a wrong interval cannot ship green and fail on the first populated symbol. Also pins that India's base is 5m and US's is 1m (a SOURCE fact: Yahoo retains 1m for seven days against 60 for 5m, so a 45-session 1m India buffer cannot be filled); that buckets are EPOCH-aligned, not first-bar-aligned (the classic chart whose candles shift when you pan); that a gap produces NO bar rather than an invented flat one; and that a mixed-basis roll-up is REFUSED, because a combined bar's volume would be partly structural zero and partly real. **Also pins the LPUSH ARGUMENT ORDER**, via a `simulateLpush` that reproduces the command's real semantics: `LPUSH key v1 v2 v3` inserts each at the head in turn, so the arguments land REVERSED. The first cut reversed before pushing, which put the OLDEST at the head — `LRANGE 0 n` would then return the oldest bars and, far worse, `LTRIM 0 cap-1` would keep the oldest `cap` entries and DROP every new bar once full, freezing the buffer at its first 45 sessions forever. No decode test could see it, because `decodeBuffer` sorts ascending on read: the output looks perfect while the store keeps the wrong end. in the pending block, and the monitor partition split FOUR ways — see below),

retyped, and a fourth cron lookup for a job with no `SCHEDULER_DEFS` row),
`tiingo-realtime-infra.test.ts` 21 → 32 (the `candles/` mirror pair),
`job-metrics-path.test.ts` 29 → 34 (the seventh Node job provisioner),
`sync-script-tier-flags.test.ts` → 10 (the Part 2 header now names two
prefixes), `candle-logic.test.ts` 62 → 74 (the intraday routing arm),
`candle-evict-logic.test.ts` 100 → 143 (the third eviction rule, then the
intraday planner/leaf fan-out and its five sizing inequalities),
`us-market-hours.test.ts` → 72 (ET session bounds, `lastCompletedUsSession`, and
the holiday table extended back to 2023), `tiingo-rt-sink-logic.test.ts` → 23
and `workers/__tests__/realtime/candle-sink.test.ts` → 18 (the ET session key),
`price-source-authority.test.ts` → 20 (`DATABENTO` 55, `TIINGO_RT` 20).

**THE HEAP TEST IS A SPAWNTEST BECAUSE TWO IN-LANE VERSIONS WERE VACUOUS, AND
BOTH WERE PROVED SO.** The loader's one property a buffering implementation
would not also satisfy is that it streams — a buffering loader maps every row
correctly. The first check used a fixed 120 MB budget and a deliberate leak
(retain every mapped row) PASSED it: 60,000 rows retain only ~12 MB, invisible
against any budget loose enough to survive GC noise, and a budget tight enough
to catch it would be flaky. Rewritten as a SCALING ratio it still passed,
because inside the shared runner the heap baseline is polluted by whatever suite
ran before it in the same process and `global.gc` is unavailable to settle it.
Measured in isolation under `--expose-gc` the same ratio separates the two
cleanly — **1.05x correct against 1.91x leaking** on a 3x input — so the ceiling
is 1.5 and the mutated loader now fails at **2.13x** with both numbers in the
message.

**Mutations that were run, and what each caught.** Reverting the checksum THROW
to the vendor's own warn-and-keep → the partial-object case. `Number(json) || 0`
on the cost quote → the non-numeric-payload case. The listing end bound compared
against the raw date instead of end-of-day → the DOW delisting-session case.
Ambiguity picking the first candidate instead of quarantining → both
recycled-ticker cases. `putCandles` before `deleteSessionRows` → the write-order
case. An unguarded `submitBatchJob` in a scanned file → the wiring scan. A
`Delete` rule under `databento/` → `edgar-infra-coverage`'s protected-root
regression. **Removing the D1 timeframe guard → three cases, which is the one
worth keeping**: it proves the RANK TABLE ALONE does not refuse a daily
displacement (DATABENTO does outrank TIINGO_RT), so the timeframe test beside it
is load-bearing rather than decorative.

**The repo's NUL tripwire caught this branch.** `databento-session-writer.ts`
shipped a LITERAL 0x00 at byte 5960 in its session key — in a file whose own
comment states the escape convention, which is the "naming a bug is not
protection from it" shape exactly. `market-fields-reader.test.ts` failed with
the byte offset; it is `\u0000` now.

**THE GUARD ITSELF HAD A HOLE, AND ADDING THIS VENDOR IS WHAT FOUND IT.**
`no-feed-fetch-bypass.test.ts` matched `fetch(`, `fetchWithTimeout(`,
`import ky` and `deps.httpGet(`. It did not match
`const f = globalThis.fetch; await f(url)` — the call site is a plain identifier
and the capture is a property read, so a file could name a FEED_HOST, download
gigabytes from it, and scan as making ZERO HTTP calls. It surfaced because
`databento-client.ts`'s exemption claimed two call sites and the scan reported
none. Two patterns were added (`globalThis.fetch capture` and
`injected fetchImpl()`), the synthetic control was extended to cover the
captured-global idiom, and removing either pattern now fails three subtests.

**THE PROBE SPENDS THROUGH THE LEDGER, NOT AROUND IT.** `databento-probe.ts` has
its own $0.05 cap and a TTY prompt with no `--yes`, and neither is a substitute
for the budget guard: the source scan caught its `submitBatchJob(` outside a
`withDatabentoBudget(` frame, which is the MONEY-1309 shape exactly. It now
writes a `purpose: "PROBE"` inventory row like any other purchase, and gains
idempotency as a side effect — a second probe of the same window reuses the row
instead of paying twice.

**TWO DEFECTS THE TESTS FOUND IN CODE THAT TYPE-CHECKED.** `resolveShard` built
`"${index}/${count}"` from two environment variables, so an absent
`CLOUD_RUN_TASK_INDEX` produced `"/4"`; the obvious repair — defaulting to 0 —
would have had every task of an execution claim shard 0, load the same files,
and leave three quarters of the batch unloaded at four times the cost. It now
reads the two separately and REFUSES a count above 1 with no index. And the
coverage aggregation passed `{ $date: <millis> }` to `$runCommandRaw`, which
Prisma serialises through Extended JSON RELAXED mode: it reached the driver as
"Failed to convert 'JSON' to 'BSON'", an error naming neither the field nor the
shape, and only once a real database was attached. Both aggregations were then
re-run against the live QA database rather than re-type-checked.

**THE PRISMA MODEL COULD NOT EXPRESS ITS OWN WRITE ORDER.** `DatabentoBatchJob`
shipped `jobId String` REQUIRED and `@@unique([jobId])`, while
`withDatabentoBudget` creates the row in `QUOTED` BEFORE `batch.submit_job` runs
— deliberately, so a crash between the two leaves a visible row rather than
spend nobody can find. Making `jobId` optional is not enough on its own:
MongoDB's unique indexes are not sparse, a missing field indexes as `null`, and
`null` collides with `null`, so the collection would have admitted exactly ONE
un-submitted row and rejected every later one with a duplicate-key error naming
a field the operator never set. The unique moved onto the six-field window key,
which makes "a window is never bought twice" a database constraint rather than a
lookup that happens to run first.

**THE COST MODEL'S ONE MUTATION THAT SURVIVED, AND WHY.** Eight deliberate
breaks were tried against `databento-cost-model-logic.ts` and seven failed the
suite immediately: a crossed book recorded as a negative spread, a fixed 16:00
close grid, an interpolated percentile, a zero row for an empty cell, tiers
defaulting to T1, a rebuild check ignoring the year, and a FAILED version
treated as usable. The eighth PASSED — swapping `summarizeCell`'s
`cell.spread.count` for `cell.spread.values.length`, which caps every busy cell
at the reservoir's 4,096 and makes a spread built from four quotes
indistinguishable from one built from forty thousand. The reservoir's own
`count` was asserted; the JOIN through `summarizeCell` was not. That is the
"test the join, not just the halves" shape exactly, and the case now exists.

**THE MONITOR GUARD HAD TWO CATEGORIES AND NEEDED FOUR.**
`edgar-monitor-and-scheduler.spawntest.ts` partitioned every rendered monitor
into "latency" and "everything else", and applied one no-data rule to the
second: silence must page, because for a zero-write monitor silence IS the
failure. The Databento D1 tripwire is neither. It watches a counter that must
read zero forever, its emitters run Tue-Sat, and `notify_no_data: true` would
have paged every Sunday and Monday for jobs behaving perfectly — which is
exactly how `bhavcopy-sync`'s monitor got muted. The partition is now FOUR,
keyed on the comparison DIRECTION rather than on a name: a monitor firing
BELOW a threshold watches something that should be happening, so its own
silence is that failure and must page; one firing ABOVE zero watches something
that should never happen, so silence is health. Flipping `> 0` to `< 1` in the
template reclassifies it and fails the absence rule, and a fifth shape appearing
fails the coverage assertion rather than being governed by nothing.

**TWO DEFECTS FOUND BY RE-READING THE DIFF, NOT BY A FAILING TEST.**
`stepDownload` ran on the leader task AND filtered the file list by shard, so a
four-task execution fetched one quarter of the files and never requested the
rest, reporting success — downloading is a whole-JOB operation and only the
load has a partitionable unit. And the sharded load wrote the whole `files`
JSON array back, which is last-writer-wins across tasks: three quarters of a
four-task load would have vanished with every task reporting success. The load
now stamps each file through MongoDB's positional operator, verified against
the QA database rather than type-checked — including that `nModified` is 0 for
a filename that is not there, so the caller's warning path is reachable.

**AND ONE IN THE APPEND'S HIGH-WATER MARK.** It took the maximum `end` across
an entry's rows, but a symbol set above 2,000 names splits into several jobs
sharing an `entryId`. Chunk A reaching Thursday while chunk B stopped at
Tuesday would have reported Thursday, started the next run on Friday, and left
chunk B permanently short — with nothing to reveal it, because the mark had
moved past. It is the minimum across chunks now. The selection moved into
`databento-append-logic.ts` because a source scan could not distinguish
`marks[0]` from `marks[marks.length - 1]`: the mutation swapping them SURVIVED
the deploy-contract test and fails the unit test.

**A DISCOVERY LIST NOBODY CAN CHECK ROTS, AND THIS ONE HAD.**
`setup-infra.sh` provisions five things and then PRINTS what it does not cover,
so an operator knows what still has to be run by hand. That list named three of
ten scripts, and had named three since EDGAR: the Tiingo backfills, all three
XBRL jobs, BSE, doc-ingest, feed-backfill, the prod->QA mirror and both
Databento jobs were invisible to anyone reading it. Its lifecycle line still
said "the edgar/ bucket lifecycle rules" while the policy covered four prefixes
across three tickets — a description that is wrong is worse than none, because
it tells an operator the rule does not apply to them.

That is expensive rather than untidy: a Cloud Run JOB pins its image at
PROVISION time and deploying the workers SERVICE does not move it, so a script
missing from this list is a job nobody re-pins after a deploy, running whatever
it was created with, indefinitely, while the logs look healthy. MONEY-1189's fix
sat un-executed on the nightly jobs for exactly that reason. Both lists are
rebuilt from disk now and machine-checked in both directions — a provisioner
that appears and a name that outlives its script each fail.

## MONEY-1373 — the code review, and the eight guards that were decorative

A five-agent fresh-context review over the branch diff (101 files, ~21,700
insertions) returned 30+ findings. No test file was added for them; the case
counts of six existing files moved instead: `databento-harvest-logic` 50 -> 56,
`databento-append-logic` 29 -> 32, `databento-logic` 60 -> 66,
`databento-symbology` 19 -> 20, `databento-wired` 41 (rebalanced), and
`no-feed-fetch-bypass` 36 (one new synthetic control).

**A MUTATION SWEEP FOUND EIGHT SURVIVORS, and every one of them was in a
SOURCE-SCAN assertion.** The pure-logic layer took 15 mutations and caught all 15. The regex layer — `databento-wired.test.ts` and everything reachable only
through it — took 8 and caught none:

| what survived                                                       | why the scan could not see it                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| the probe's non-TTY refusal INVERTED                                | asserted `/process\.stdin\.isTTY/` — presence, not polarity     |
| the probe's spend cap widened 1000x                                 | asserted `/PROBE_MAX_USD/` — the identifier, not the comparison |
| `"QUOTED"` added to the high-water mark's terminal set              | forbade two literals, not the set                               |
| the arm hoisted to module scope as `const ARMED = isHarvestArmed()` | one regex, one spelling                                         |
| `$exists` replacing the positional filter's filename equality       | asserted the `files.$.` path, not the match                     |
| `stampFileVerified` hardcoding `verified: true`                     | asserted the call, not what it records                          |
| `process.exitCode = 1` in the cost-model catch                      | forbade only the token `throw`                                  |
| the gap computed before the range read, fed null                    | compared `indexOf` positions in the FILE, not execution order   |

The remedy each time was the one the branch already knew: EXTRACT THE DECISION.
`quoteExceedsProbeCap`, `mayPromptForSpend` and `terminalStatesFor` are now
pure functions with their own cases, exactly as `highWaterMarkFromChunks` was
extracted earlier for the same reason. Where a scan is genuinely the right tool
it was tightened to assert the property rather than a token, and each repaired
guard was re-mutated to confirm it now fails.

**One survivor is left, deliberately.** Reading the listing bound's date parts
with `getFullYear()` instead of `getUTCFullYear()` is only observable in a
negative-offset timezone; this machine is UTC+5:30 and CI is UTC, so no
assertion here can see it. The code is correct; catching it would need a
spawntest with a forced `TZ`, which is its own change.

**The heap spawntest is marginal on a loaded machine and that predates this
work.** Measured five runs per variant: the committed source fails 1 in 5
(1.98x against a 1.5 ceiling), the reviewed source 3 in 5 (1.79-1.93x). The
ceiling was NOT raised — a guard weakened to go green is worse than no guard,
and this one has already caught two real leaks. Its own design note says the
in-process versions were vacuous twice; the ratio needs a quiet machine.

| `packages/datadog/__tests__/perf-monitors-agreement.test.ts`  | 50    | `scripts/ops/datadog/apply-perf-monitors.sh` and the three `monitor-gcp-*.json` templates — the nine Pub/Sub, Cloud Run, Gemini-quota and Cloud Scheduler rows. Functional: spawns the REAL script against a stubbed `curl`, so the create-vs-update-vs-delete decision is executed rather than grepped. **Scope is asserted from both sides**: every `gcp.pubsub.*` / `gcp.run.*` query names its subscription or its service, the only `{*}` body is the Gemini quota row that argues for it, and the FATAL guard is proven to live in the SCRIPT — a row whose scope is mutated to `*` makes the dry run itself exit 1, not merely this file go red. **Units are the other half.** `request_latency.user_execution.p95` is a SUB-METRIC and is queried with `avg:`, never `p95:` (which asks for a distribution that does not exist); the latency thresholds are asserted `> 100000` so a future `540` written in seconds is red where `540000` is right; and the Pub/Sub age threshold is checked to sit under the 600s ack deadline and above `RUN_TIME_BUDGET_MS`, read out of `stock-document-extract-logic.ts` rather than retyped. **The preflight's THREE outcomes are driven separately**: a series with no points refuses that row BY NAME and leaves eight writes behind, a preflight that could not RUN writes nothing at all, and the two must differ by MESSAGE and not only by exit code — collapsing them is how one 403 becomes "the series is empty". The failure RATIO preflights its DENOMINATOR and never its numerator, because no 5xx anywhere is the healthy estate and a healthy estate must not be a reason to skip creating the alarm; the scheduler row preflights the UN-SLICED log series, because `severity:error` is empty on a good day. Plus: an absent warning is ABSENT rather than the `Number("") === 0` that would read as a permanently-breached warning on a `> 0` monitor, every threshold is a NUMBER and not the string `dd_render` was handed, no message carries a BARE `{{value}}` (`dd_render`'s final guard kills the whole body over one) while the grouped rows still carry the dotted `{{subscription_id.name}}` that survives it, the tags carry this script's own namespace and no other script's, a second run UPDATES all nine and creates none, an orphan under this tag is DELETED, a `--dry-run` neither lists nor prunes, and `--only=verify` exits 3 on each of the three drifts — a name only in code, a stranger only in Datadog, and a monitor whose title still matches but whose QUERY was edited in the UI. **Four more came out of the code review, each a silent-miss class.** SPACE aggregation is chosen per metric and asserted per metric: `instance_count` carries a `state` tag (active/idle) so `max:` reads max(active, idle) — a service at its cap of 20 as 12 active + 8 idle evaluates to 12 and never crosses `> 18` — and `pending_requests` is per-REVISION with two overlapping on every deploy, so both SUM while an AGE still uses `max` because the oldest message IS the question; the BOARD is held to the same aggregation as the monitor, since a board drawn with `max:` beside a monitor evaluated with `sum:` is two answers to one question and the board is what somebody checks first. The dead-letter row preflights the CRAWL and not its own series — measured, `dead_letter_message_count` on a quiet subscription returns NO SERIES AT ALL rather than a zero, so preflighting it would refuse the row on exactly the healthy estate it watches. And a preflight refusal SUPPRESSES THE PRUNE entirely: a refused row never reaches the rendered set, so pruning would delete its live monitor — one transient hour of a vendor crawl not reporting would destroy a monitor, its history and its mute state, as the only lasting effect of a run that reports failure. **A SECOND review pass added five more.** The managed listing is ENV-SCOPED (`monitor_tags` ANDs comma-separated tags), because without it a qa run's listing contained the PRODUCTION monitors and the prune deleted them — rows 4-9 are prod-only and skip without reaching the rendered set, exactly like a refused row, but `FAILED` stays empty so the refused-row guard did not catch it; the stub models the API's tag filter so an unscoped listing still returns everything and the case fails against the old code. `instance_count` groups by `revision_name` as well as service, because maxScale is a per-REVISION annotation and two revisions overlap on every deploy, so a service-level sum crosses 18 while neither revision is near its own cap — a false page on every rollout in place of a silent miss. And `dd_verify_managed`'s EXCLUSIVE flag is VALIDATED and its value pinned per call site: a caller who omits it consumes the first rendered NAME as the flag, dropping that name from the code side into the ignored bucket and reporting in sync while under-reporting by one. **A THIRD pass added five more**, because each round kept finding a defect inside the last round's fixes. Grouping by `revision_name` had to come with `notify_no_data: false` on those two rows: a revision name changes on every release and the retired revision stops emitting within minutes (measured — two revisions in 24h, the older one's series already ended), so Datadog's ~24h group retention turns no-data into a page on every DEPLOY that re-notifies hourly — the false page that grouping by revision was introduced to remove, through the other door; a companion case proves the crawl-alive signal still lives on four rows that group by nothing ephemeral. Those rows are preflighted BY THE GROUP, since "the metric has points" says nothing about whether the crawl imports `revision_name` and a `by {}` over an unimported tag returns zero series. And `LIST_TAG` is pinned to contain the MANAGED tag as well as the env — dropping the managed half is a plausible "simplification" that would list every monitor tagged `env:production` and prune the ~79 belonging to the other two scripts, which is the same wipe from the other direction; the stub models BOTH tag terms so that case fails on the consequence rather than the spelling |
| `workers/__tests__/processors/sync-shard-guards.test.ts`      | 6     | `workers/src/processors/sync.ts` — the broker-sync SHARD LEAF. The scheduled trigger fans out to 64 leaves and prod holds 9 connections across 6 buckets, so **58 leaves of every fan-out matched nothing**, threw "No broker connections found", answered 500, were redelivered five times, dead-lettered and notified the founder: 3,733 5xx and 928 dead-letters a day, 97.6% of that subscription, for work that did not need doing. These are SOURCE guards BY CHOICE and the file says why — `processSync` imports Prisma, `@usemoney/security`, the broker adapters, Datadog and the e-mail templates at module load, and the DECISIONS are already exercised pure in `broker-sync.test.ts`, so what is left is WIRING: each property here is the presence or absence of a NAMED FIELD in a NAMED CALL, which is the one shape a scan reads exactly (unlike the `marks[0]`-vs-`marks[len-1]` class it cannot tell apart). Pins that the leaf does **NOT** return early — a guard against a fix that was written and withdrawn: returning as soon as `connectionCount === 0` reads as a harmless optimisation (it skips a metrics loop over an empty array and two cheap queries) but also skips the per-bucket RE-PAIRING, which has nothing to do with broker connections and covers users whose trades arrived by CSV import; they would simply have stopped being paired, silently. ## MONEY-1402 — the suite stopped asserting against the wall clock

`packages/core/__tests__/screener/market-fields-reader.test.ts` **19 → 32**. The
19 was stale by more than this change; 32 is measured.

**`main` was RED when this started, and not from anyone's branch.** Every
market-structure read is bounded `date >= now - MARKET_FIELD_LOOKBACK_DAYS`, so
a dated fixture with no injected clock does not assert a behaviour — it asserts
how long ago somebody typed the date. `day("2026-08-14")` sat behind the 30-day
`derivatives` window and went red on **2026-09-13**, thirty days later, with
nothing changed but the calendar. Because the push gate runs the full suite,
that failed every branch, and on each one it looked like a fresh unrelated
regression.

The file already had the convention — `const NOW` and a pinned `now` on every
direct `loadMarketFieldValues` call. What it could not pin was the two exported
entry points: `applyMarketStructureFilters` took no `now` and `runScreener` had
no way to pass one down, so five assertions ran against `Date.now()`. Four more
were fused behind the 45- and 60-day windows, due 2026-09-28 and 2026-10-13.

`ScreenerDeps.now` and a fourth parameter on `applyMarketStructureFilters` make
the existing seam reachable. **The acceptance was never "passes today"** — a fix
that only passes today has changed nothing — so it is measured with the clock
shifted: 32/32 at +0d, +365d, +3650d and +36500d, and the whole `packages/core`
suite is 7,347/7,347 at +365d, which is what establishes no sibling file has the
same shape.

Three of the 32 are the guard, and they fail **TODAY** rather than on some future
morning: the file scans its own source for a call site that lets `now` default,
proves that scan finds the call sites it polices before asserting anything about
them, and pins the three lookback constants that a narrowed window would
silently invalidate. Mutations held red under the REAL clock — unpinning a
`runScreener` call, unpinning a `loadMarketFieldValues` call, and narrowing
`derivatives` 30 → 20 — and under a shifted clock the unpinned call fails the
behavioural assertions too.

## MONEY-1406 — the CI gate got correct, then got fast

`apps/web/__tests__/ci/verify-gate-parity.test.ts` **7 → 10**.

**The gate was red for a reason that was not a test failure.** PR #420's `yarn
test` reported `# pass 20866, # fail 0, # cancelled 1, exit 1` —
`__tests__/cache/wrapper.test.ts` cancelled at the 30s timeout. That file is 21
cases with no timers and runs in **3.3s locally**. It did not get slow, it got
starved: `apps/web` pinned `--test-concurrency=4` against a 2-vCPU runner.

That literal `4` was itself a fix for the same failure from the other side — on
a 14-core Mac at node's default concurrency, five files (four of them under
`cache/`, the same family) cancelled at 30s. **One constant cannot be right on
both machines**, so it is now `min(4, availableParallelism())`: still 4 on the
Mac, 2 on the runner. Third instance of the class; the first two were fixed
per-instance, this closes the rule. `--test-timeout` is deliberately unchanged —
it is the only thing that can catch a genuinely hung test.

**Separately**, the serialized step took 21m59s, of which `@usemoney/web` was
607s of 1319s. The job is now a 2-way matrix, web against everything else,
607 vs 712 and needing no finer split. **Sharding fixes wall clock and nothing
else** — turbo already ran the workspaces sequentially, so web had the whole
runner to itself when it starved, and a second runner would not have saved it.

The three added cases guard the split rather than the speed: a merge gate is
only safe to shard while the shards cover every workspace exactly once, and a
package in NEITHER shard stops being tested with nothing to say so. Checked
STRUCTURALLY — the filters must be exact complements, `--filter=X` and
`--filter=!X` — which holds for any future workspace graph, so a new package
lands in `rest` by construction rather than falling through. Mutations held red:
breaking the complement (`!web` → `!core`), adding a third shard, dropping
`--concurrency=1`, and dropping the filter entirely.

## MONEY-1499 — the int8 embedding migration (+5 files / +81 cases)

B8, executing `docs/reference/embeddings-decision-2026-09.md` §5. Every test
below runs with no Atlas, no Mongo, no network and no embedding quota: the pure
modules take their inputs, the manifest test reads the real committed JSON, and
the schema test reads `schema.prisma` and the source tree off disk.

The defect class this whole ticket sits in is SILENT: a wrong BSON subtype is
simply not indexed, `quantization: "scalar"` over an int8 field makes Atlas skip
every vector, and a quantization that does not preserve cosine ORDER produces a
search that answers plausibly and ranks wrongly. None of those raise. So the
assertions are about what is true when nothing is reported.

Pins that `quantization` over int8 is REFUSED by name, that int8 accepts cosine (the gate B0 §5 left open, closed against the vendor's own supported-similarity table) and that int1 does not. The cases that earn their place are the ones a looser gate would have passed: an EMPTY run (two averages compared with `>=` make a population of zero read OK for ever), a run short of the fixed 50-query set, a v2 returning FEWER rows (overlap divides by K, not by the smaller set — otherwise a collapsed index that returns one row v1 also had scores a perfect 1.0), and a latency comparison with nothing on the v1 side. Also pins that an undecodable row is DROPPED and COUNTED rather than scored 0 — a 0 sorts last and reads as a weak match, which is a lie about a row that was never read.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | `packages/core/__tests__/embeddings-v2-read.test.ts`            | 10         | PASS   |

**Not unit-tested, and why.** `scripts/jobs/embeddings-v2-backfill.ts`,
`scripts/ops/apply-atlas-search-indexes.ts` and `scripts/ops/embeddings-parity.ts`
are I/O shells that call `main()` at module top level — the Cloud Run entry-point
convention — so importing one from a test would open a real database connection.
Every decision they make lives in the three pure modules above. The runtime proof
they need is not a unit test but `apply-atlas-search-indexes.ts --probe`, which
answers the two questions no test can: whether a subtype-9 binary survives
`$runCommandRaw` intact, and whether Atlas accepts a BinData `queryVector`
through it.

## fix/MONEY-1608 — lake jobs that cannot end silently, and run in-region (+4 files, 23-Sep-2026)

MONEY-1608 and MONEY-1609. `lake-replay-us` ran for 8 hours, loaded 0 months
and exited **0**: an upload stream settled neither way, the awaited promise held
no handle, and Node emptied its event loop with `main()` still pending. Counts
are the EXECUTED `# tests` of a single-file run, as in the MONEY-1544 section;
`job-completion.spawntest.ts` declares 5 `it(` and runs 13.

| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ------ |
| `packages/storage/src/index.ts` `settleWriteStream` (MONEY-1608) — settles exactly once: `finish` resolves, `error` rejects, `close` before `finish` rejects, and the deadline rejects on its own and destroys the stream; the real SDK's finish-before-close order. The mutants reproduce the incident's signature ("Promise resolution is still pending but the event loop has already resolved").                                                                                           | `packages/storage/__tests__/settle-write-stream.test.ts`  | 6          | PASS   |
| `packages/storage/src/index.ts` `uploadFile({ retries, createOnly })` (MONEY-1608) — through the real SDK against a local server: a connection reset is retried (the SDK never retries an upload without a generation precondition, `maxRetries` 0, so the retries are ours); a 403 is never retried; `createOnly` sends `ifGenerationMatch=0`; a refused re-attempt is accepted when the object holds the same bytes and thrown when it does not; there is no read-back without `createOnly`. | `packages/storage/__tests__/upload-retries.test.ts`       | 6          | PASS   |
| `packages/core/src/ops/job-completion.ts` `guardCompletion` (MONEY-1608) — spawned for real: a `main()` that never settles exits **3** with `ENDED WITHOUT COMPLETING`; one that resolves exits 0 silently; one that rejects keeps exit 1; all nine lake jobs are wired, the list derived from the directory rather than typed.                                                                                                                                                                | `packages/core/__tests__/ops/job-completion.spawntest.ts` | 13         | PASS   |
| `packages/core/src/ops/transient-error.ts` `isTransientError` (MONEY-1608 review) — retries are TRANSIENT-ONLY: network error codes, HTTP 408 / 429 / 5xx however the client carries the status, and our own deadline; a permanent error (a 403, a bad request) fails at once. Plus the `lake-replay-us` wiring: its per-symbol read retry asks this, not a blanket catch.                                                                                                                     | `packages/core/__tests__/ops/transient-error.test.ts`     | 8          | PASS   |
